replying_to: Replying to Patchwise Sparse Dictionary Learning from pre-trained Neural Network Activation Maps for Anomaly Detection in Images
display_title: Official Review of Paper1731 by Reviewer hCgd

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work combines sparse representation learning and a pre-trained neural network for classification purposes. Firstly, meaningful representation features are extracted and a sparse dictionary of the most expressive ones is built, which only come from the images without anomalies. Then, the images having anomalies will either contain a non-sparse representation as linear combination of the dictionary elements or a high reconstruction error.
content.main_review:
Whilst this is a workable solution, the paper in fact is a continuation of the original work of Napoletano et al. (2018). While Napoletano's paper built their dictionary out of a PCA and K-Means of latent representation features,  the current paper uses K-SVD, which is quite straightforward in terms of research concepts. 

The authors of the current paper argue that their approach is more robust than the other state of the arts, enabling them to drop the one-class learning scenarios and dealing with more significant variances. However, intermediate results and reasoning/proof of why the introduction of K-SVD helps reducing the variances are missing in this paper. 

On the other hand, the authors argue that combining different layers activation maps is to maximize the detection capability of the pipeline. It is not clear whether or not the performance boosting is due to the transfer learning itself or the combination of different features. The ablation experiments are not set up to answer this question.

Finally, the reviewer believes that this paper is an examination over the integration of several state of the arts schemes instead the presentation of a piece of fully novel idea. If this is true, then the impact and generalisation of the current paper are limited.
content.summary_of_the_review: Due to the lack of novel and significant theoretical and experimental discovery, this paper will not be accepted for publication. Moving forward, it is expected that this paper may be driven towards investigating how the extracted features influence each other in the context of deep learning architectures, and what features may play a major role on the performance boosting. The structured or stochastic behaviours of different features may be worth investigating.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.comment:
We would like to thank the reviewer for taking the time to analyze our work and providing us with constructive feedback.

We also would like to answer the two points raised in the review.

> On the other hand, the authors argue that combining different layers activation maps is to maximize the detection capability of the pipeline. It is not clear whether or not the performance boosting is due to the transfer learning itself or the combination of different features. > Finally, the reviewer believes that this paper is an examination over the integration of several state of the arts schemes instead the presentation of a piece of fully novel idea. If this is true, then the impact and generalisation of the current paper are limited

As stated in response to (first)[https://openreview.net/forum?id=9LJkfH5rtc&noteId=71hVCplXcVq] and (second review)[https://openreview.net/forum?id=9LJkfH5rtc&noteId=8Bq7XjH26x9], and is acknowledged by other reviewers, we are the first to combine sparse dictionary learning algorithm and transfer learning for anomaly detection. While technical novelty is not the central aspect of our work, we think that empirical evidence points towards a significant impact of our strategy as tested in different contexts; this element was not known in advance. We can not simply ignore the fact that our pipeline works with SOTA-level performance.
From a theoretical perspective, sparse coding could become a de facto standard when addressing redundancy of information in deep learning tasks, replacing often over-used PCA.

content.title: response to the novelty claim
content.comment:
The authors have stated that "we are the first to combine sparse dictionary learning algorithm and transfer learning for anomaly detection". The proposed algorithm may be the first one to apply the combination of sparse dictionary learning and transfer learning to anomaly detection - this is still arguable though. However, this combination concept has been explored and discussed in several previous works:
(1) http://proceedings.mlr.press/v28/maurer13.pdf
(2) https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2021.687496/full
(3) https://www.eecs.qmul.ac.uk/~sgg/papers/PengEtAl_CVPR2016.pdf
The reviewer cannot agree with the authors for the novelty claim.

replying_to: Replying to response to the novelty claim

content.title: On the novelty claim
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for pointing out these interesting works. We have already modified the Introduction Section to acknowledge their early (even if one of them is almost contemporary to our work) adoption of sparse dictionary learning and transfer learning. 

Nevertheless, the first work applied these techniques in the context of multi-task learning. The second and third papers dealt with transferring knowledge acquired on a "source domain" to a "target domain", working on paired datasets. Their works are closer to the domain adaptation topic. While the second paper adopted this strategy to solve a classification task over images, none of the two tackled the anomaly detection task from an unsupervised perspective.

Because of these reasons, we think that our claim of novelty is still valid, and the information provided by the reviewer confirms this claim.

replying_to: Replying to Patchwise Sparse Dictionary Learning from pre-trained Neural Network Activation Maps for Anomaly Detection in Images
display_title: Official Review of Paper1731 by Reviewer dADN

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an anomaly detection algorithm based on dictionary learning on the representations obtained by pre-trained deep convolutional networks. More precisely, the authors consider location-specific signals from a collection of training images, extracted via pre-trained neural networks of different depth and types. They then train a dictionary via K-SVD to obtain sparse representation for these patches, which are then modeled via multivariate Gaussian distribution. At testing time, the representation for each patch is computed, and a metric is computed over all patches to declare an image as an outlier/anomalous, or normal.
content.main_review:
The presented method is intuitive, and interesting. This reviewer found the following concerns, which I would appreciate the authors responding to:

The formulation of the dictionary learning problem in Eq.(1) is problematic. First, there is a dimension mismatch (since the dimensions of DX do not match those of S). Second, one of the key advantages of dictionary learning is that they allow for flexibility. In particular, they allow for overcomplete dictionaries, which in turns allows for sparser representations than say, complete, basis. That is, typically one has that the dimension of the signal, n, is smaller than the number of atoms in the dictionary, m; i.e, n<m. Here, the authors chose to make the dictionary square. Why was this choice made? Perhaps the authors wanted to limit the number of atoms in the dictionary based on computational constraints, but then why not choose m<n (which is also possible)?

The comment on page 3 that "the dictionary learning [problem] is an underdetermined linear system problem" is incorrect. The dictionary learning problem is a bi-linear (and non-convex) problem, which is not underdetermined as long as the number of examples is greater than the number of dictionary atoms (as is the case here).

The authors mention that, to their knowledge, they are the first in employing dictionary learning ideas on representations computed by neural networks. I do not think this is correct, in light of the following works, not in the context of anomaly detection but in computer vision problems in general (which resulting from a quick search - arguably many more exist):

Tang, Hao, et al. "When dictionary learning meets deep learning: Deep dictionary learning and coding network for image recognition with limited data." IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems 32.5 (2020): 2129-2141.
Zarka, John, et al. "Deep network classification by scattering and homotopy dictionary learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:1910.03561 (2019).
The reported experimental results seem good, but the experimental validation is not fully convincing: i) Why was not PatchCore inclueded in the comparison on Table 4, or on the BeanTech Anomaly Detection Dataset? In the same vein, why was not PaDim included in the BeanTech Dataset? ii) The authors mention that the feature extractors used for their method and the ones they compare to are different. In light of this, it is difficult to understand whether the difference in performance comes from just a better feature extractor. iii) On section 3.2.2. the authors mention that the "seeds have been changed from run to run". This is somewhat concerning, as it seems to imply that the seed of the random number generator might have been fixed in previous experiments. Please clarify on the experimental setting.
content.summary_of_the_review: The approach is intuitive, though some technical aspects and choices unclear. Some aspects of the numerical experiments likewise require clarification.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1731 by Reviewer dADN

content.title: Response to Reviewer dADN
content.comment:
We would like to thank the reviewer for taking the time to analyze our work and providing us with constructive feedback.

We also would like to answer the different questions raised in the review.

> The formulation of the dictionary learning problem in Eq.(1) is problematic. First, there is a dimension mismatch (since the dimensions of DX do not match those of S). Second, one of the key advantages of dictionary learning is that they allow for flexibility. In particular, they allow for overcomplete dictionaries, which in turns allows for sparser representations than say, complete, basis. That is, typically one has that the dimension of the signal, n, is smaller than the number of atoms in the dictionary, m; i.e, n<m. Here, the authors chose to make the dictionary square. Why was this choice made? Perhaps the authors wanted to limit the number of atoms in the dictionary based on computational constraints, but then why not choose m<n (which is also possible)?

> The comment on page 3 that "the dictionary learning [problem] is an underdetermined linear system problem" is incorrect. 

We would like to answer both remarks above. We will correct the dimension mismatch in Eq.(1).  We apologize for the mistake we did referring to the sparse dictionary problem as an underdetermined linear system. We wanted to indicate the [sparse coding problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparse_approximation). For the same reason, to keep this problem as simple as possible (from a dimensional perspective) and close to its ideal setting, we took the Dictionary to be squared.

> The authors mention that, to their knowledge, they are the first in employing dictionary learning ideas on representations computed by neural networks. I do not think this is correct, in light of the following works, not in the context of anomaly detection but in computer vision problems in general (which resulting from a quick search - arguably many more exist).

We are the first to adopt the combination of these techniques to address images anomaly detection, as recognized by other reviewers.

> i) Why was not PatchCore inclueded in the comparison on Table 4, or on the BeanTech Anomaly Detection Dataset? In the same vein, why was not PaDim included in the BeanTech Dataset?

As stated in response to the [second review](https://openreview.net/forum?id=9LJkfH5rtc&noteId=8Bq7XjH26x9), we propose to extend experiments of section 3.2.4 on PaDiM and section 3.2.3 on PatchCore and PaDiM. Moreover, we can propose to run another set of experiments on the Kolektor Surface-Defect Dataset. We could also extend PatchCore to Rd-MVTec dataset, but it could require more time than we have currently available.

> ii) The authors mention that the feature extractors used for their method and the ones they compare to are different. In light of this, it is difficult to understand whether the difference in performance comes from just a better feature extractor.

We have shown for each method the solution with the best backbone network identified by the authors for that particular dataset.

> iii) On section 3.2.2. the authors mention that the "seeds have been changed from run to run". This is somewhat concerning, as it seems to imply that the seed of the random number generator might have been fixed in previous experiments. Please clarify on the experimental setting.

We ran all the experiments with different seeds (3), and the results were never significantly different. We will add this detail to the paper. We have only highlighted the fact of the seeds in section 3.2.2. because in that case, the randomization process is a core aspect, and we opted for an overall increased number of runs.

replying_to: Replying to Patchwise Sparse Dictionary Learning from pre-trained Neural Network Activation Maps for Anomaly Detection in Images
display_title: Official Review of Paper1731 by Reviewer xLeb

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper presents an anomaly detection and localization method based upon sparse dictionary learning on the activations of a pretrained neural network.  The method uses the K-SVD algorithm and modified OMP to solve the sparse coding problem.  The method is compared on industrial anomaly datasets and shows state of the art performance on detection w/ respect to other published work.  

The contributions of the paper are the use of dictionary learning on the output of a pretrained CNN.
State of the art anomaly detection on industrial datasets.
Extensive justification of hyper parameter/layer decisions of the model.
content.main_review:
This paper reads very well and tackles a niche problem of industrial anomaly detection.  The methods are well defined and experiments support the conclusion.  

+I believe the main contribution of this paper is the use of dictionary learning on the output features of a pretrained CNN.  The paper claims to be the first to investigate this methodology for anomaly detection.  To my knowledge, I also do not know of published methods that have done this, and I view this as a novel contribution.

+The paper states that the best scores are coming with a combination of activation maps at different layers.  I think this makes intuitive sense.  Dictionary elements learned at multiple scales should contribute different information to the anomaly detection method.

My main criticism of the work was applicability, scope, and impact.  While the authors do a good job scoping the paper to this problem, I am left wanting more.  Yes, the contribution is there and it is publishable.  But I am not convinced of the impact of the work to the extend that it belongs at ICLR.  

-The paper could benefit from additional experimental results on real world examples.  At least one more datasets over the industrial type datasets, something at a larger scale. 
- While there are many empirical experiments to justify the hyper parameters of the system, I feel that it detracts from novelty.  Parameter grid search is a fine thing when optimizing a system, but I would have liked a stronger discussion on the benefits and contributions that dictionary learning has/ and could have in this context.  What does this give you conceptually?  Sparse coding gives you sparse vectors, it gives you selectivity of elements, and it gives you greater expressiveness... how do these concepts transform the problem and impact how or why this should be used in the community?  I feel like this would be the connection I would need for me to get really excited about this paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: I have expressed most of my justification in the main review.  Basically, I like the paper, I think it is scoped really well for this problem.  It makes incremental contributions and novelty and is comparable to the state of the art.  It is publishable in its current form.  However for ICLR I would have liked to see additional impact and discussion on the innovativeness of the method.  I would de-emphasize the grid search of hyper parameters and rather see why this is a good idea in the first place, why it should be adopted in this type of problem in general, and how this could impact the field at large.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.details_of_ethics_concerns: I have no concerns on ethics.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1731 by Reviewer xLeb

content.title: Response to Reviewer xLeb
content.comment:
We would like to thank the reviewer for taking the time to analyze our work and providing us with constructive feedback.

We would like to answer two observations mainly:

> While there are many empirical experiments to justify the hyper parameters of the system, I feel that it detracts from novelty. Parameter grid search is a fine thing when optimizing a system, but I would have liked a stronger discussion on the benefits and contributions that dictionary learning has/ and could have in this context. What does this give you conceptually? Sparse coding gives you sparse vectors, it gives you selectivity of elements, and it gives you greater expressiveness... how do these concepts transform the problem and impact how or why this should be used in the community? I feel like this would be the connection I would need for me to get really excited about this paper.

We would like to remark that the studies we have conducted over the different architectures and the possibility of combining different layers are necessary to fully comprehend our method's potential. We then report here what we wrote for the [first review](https://openreview.net/forum?id=9LJkfH5rtc&noteId=IC8wZ8s5qWA) since we think it can answer some questions posed by the reviewer:

> Our work is strictly related to the concept of sparsity in signals. While [PatchCore](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.08265) and [PaDiM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.08785) used a non-structured approach to achieve information reduction, we proposed to address it as a well-known mathematical problem. We think that the channels dimension of features activation maps is full of redundant information. Instead of randomly reducing its dimensions (as done in PaDiM) or adopting a sub-sampling procedure (as done in PatchCore), we thought that information could be appropriately filtered in a rigorous way. This aspect is even more interesting because each learned dictionary achieves a multimodal input representation as we are not operating in a one-class learning scenario. We claim that features as so many, we could run an experiment with a greedy sparse K-SVD with OMP sparsity level of 1/100 the number of channels and still end up with relevant scores on MVTec. The reduction operation we perform allows us to occupy way less memory when storing dictionaries with respect to PatchCore and PaDiM. Last but not least, every reviewer agreed that we are the first to combine transfer learning and sparse dictionary encoding in an end-to-end pipeline for anomaly detection. While technical novelty is not the central aspect of our work, we think that empirical evidence points towards a significant impact of our strategy as tested in different contexts; this element was not known in advance. Sparse coding could become a de facto standard when addressing redundancy of information in deep learning tasks, replacing often over-used PCA.

The second observation we would like to address is the following:

> - The paper could benefit from additional experimental results on real-world examples. At least one more datasets over the industrial type datasets, something at a larger scale.

As already stated in response to the [first review](https://openreview.net/forum?id=9LJkfH5rtc&noteId=IC8wZ8s5qWA), we propose an extension of experiments of section 3.2.4 on PaDiM and section 3.2.3 on PatchCore and PaDiM. Moreover, we can propose to run another set of experiments on [Kolektor Surface-Defect Dataset](https://paperswithcode.com/dataset/kolektorsdd). 

While we appreciate the reviewer's comments inquiring about the impact of our work on the scientific community, we do not understand why the reviewer marked Correctness as "1: The main claims of the paper are incorrect or not at all supported by theory or empirical results." There is no evidence of arguments to support this claim in the review itself.

replying_to: Replying to Patchwise Sparse Dictionary Learning from pre-trained Neural Network Activation Maps for Anomaly Detection in Images
display_title: Official Review of Paper1731 by Reviewer Az8x

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper tackles image anomaly detection by CNNs as feature extraction and sparse dictionary learning as its classifier solved by KSVD. In reference, the sparse coding can be effectively solved by OMP and its reconstruction errors denote the anomaly scores of images. As this paper states,  it is the first work to use a sparse dictionary learning algorithm to handle deep network features. Also, the proposed method achieves the sota performance.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
This paper well describes the main pipeline and one can easily tell the technical details without confusion. Overall, it is technically correct. In addition, the ablation studies and comparison on multiple benchmarks are sufficient to evaluate the proposed sparse dictionary learning pipeline.

Weaknesses:
As far as I know, sparse coding and dictionary learning has been well investigated on anomaly detection of both images and videos, though deep neural networks as feature extraction are rarely adopted. The KSVD and OMP used in this paper are classical algorithms on sparse coding and dictionary learning. Thus, I am much concerned about the technical novelty of the proposed pipeline, which simply combines deep features and sparse coding formulation.

Also, the sota performance claimed in this paper is unfair because recent advanced work on MVTec is missing.
content.summary_of_the_review: I prefer to reject this paper with the concerns of technical novelty and sota performance claimed in this paper.

We would like to thank the reviewer for taking the time to analyze our work and providing us with constructive feedbacks.

We would like to answer two observations mainly: 

> Thus, I am much concerned about the technical novelty of the proposed pipeline, which simply combines deep features and sparse coding formulation.

Our work is strictly related to the concept of sparsity in signals. While [PatchCore](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.08265) and [PaDiM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.08785) used a non-structured approach to achieve information reduction, we proposed to address it as a well-known mathematical problem. We think that the channels dimension of features activation maps is full of redundant information. Instead of randomly reducing its dimensions (as done in PaDiM) or adopting a sub-sampling procedure (as done in PatchCoe), we thought that information could be appropriately filtered in a rigorous way. This aspect is even more interesting because each learned dictionary achieves a multimodal input representation as we are not operating in a one-class learning scenario.

We claim that features as so many, we could run an experiment with a greedy sparse K-SVD with OMP sparsity level of 1/100 the number of channels and still end up with relevant scores on MVTec. The reduction operation we perform allows us to occupy way less memory when storing dictionaries with respect to PatchCore and PaDiM.

Last but not least, every reviewer agreed that we are the first to combine transfer learning and sparse dictionary encoding in an end-to-end pipeline for anomaly detection. While technical novelty is not the central aspect of our work, we think that empirical evidence points towards a significant impact of our strategy as tested in different contexts; this element was not known in advance. Sparse coding could become a de facto standard when addressing redundancy of information in deep learning tasks, replacing often over-used PCA.

> Also, the sota performance claimed in this paper is unfair because recent advanced work on MVTec is missing.

We agree with the reviewer that we did non report all the current methods, but still, we have chosen the best one, according to [PapersWithCode](https://paperswithcode.com/sota/anomaly-detection-on-mvtec-ad), which is a well-known source. We think the reviewer's observation is incorrect because we compared our method against the best methods of 2020 and 2021, respectively. 
The link also shows that our method would still be top 10 between those developed in the last two years for MVTec AD dataset. If the reviewer thinks it is more appropriate to show all results, we can easily add them. The reviewer does not comment on the performance of our method on other datasets, where we overcome proposed methodologies. To ensure an even more fair comparison, we propose an extension of experiments of section 3.2.4 on PaDiM and section 3.2.3 on PatchCore and PaDiM.
